title: SEBI Will Pilot Tokenised Corporate Bonds Within Nine Months. India's $560 Billion Debt Market Is Getting a Blockchain Upgrade.
excerpt: The regulator also wants bond issuers to disclose as much as equity-listed companies. Both changes could open the market to retail investors for the first time.
body:
India's securities regulator just announced that it will pilot blockchain-based tokenisation of corporate bonds within six to nine months — a move that could transform how the country's $560 billion debt market settles trades and could eventually give retail investors access to a market that has been dominated by institutions since independence.

## What SEBI Announced

Securities and Exchange Board of India chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey told an industry event on Tuesday that SEBI is preparing a pilot program to tokenise corporate bonds using distributed ledger technology. The pilot would test near-instant settlement of bond trades — a dramatic improvement over the current T+1 or T+2 settlement cycle that has long been a barrier to liquidity in the corporate debt market.

Tokenisation means converting traditional securities into digital tokens on a shared ledger. Each token represents a fractional ownership claim on the underlying bond. Trades settle atomically — ownership and payment move simultaneously, eliminating counterparty risk and reducing the operational overhead that has kept smaller investors out of the market for decades.

Pandey also announced that SEBI is reviewing whether listed debt securities should be subject to the same disclosure requirements as listed equities. Currently, bond issuers face lighter reporting obligations, which investors and analysts have long argued creates an information asymmetry that suppresses secondary market trading volumes and makes price discovery unreliable.

## Why This Matters

India's corporate bond market has grown from ₹17.5 lakh crore to ₹59 lakh crore in recent years, but it remains remarkably shallow compared to the equity markets. Between 85% and 90% of all issuances are concentrated in AA or AAA-rated entities — the safest credits with the lowest yields. The secondary market is thin, with most bonds held to maturity by insurance companies and pension funds rather than actively traded.

The problem is structural. Settlement is slow. Price discovery is poor. Retail participation is negligible. And the disclosure framework means investors often have less information about a company's debt than about its equity — even though debt sits higher in the capital structure and is theoretically the safer investment.

Tokenisation addresses the first problem directly. If bonds settle in near real-time on a shared ledger, the friction that keeps institutional investors from trading frequently — and retail investors from participating at all — largely disappears. Fractional ownership becomes technically feasible, which could lower the minimum investment threshold from the current ₹10 lakh face value that effectively locks out individual investors.

## The Blockchain Distinction

India's relationship with blockchain technology has been complicated. The Reserve Bank of India banned banks from servicing cryptocurrency exchanges in 2018, a decision the Supreme Court overturned in 2020. Since then, the government has imposed a 30% tax on crypto gains and a 1% TDS on transactions, effectively freezing retail crypto trading volumes.

But SEBI's tokenisation pilot is not about cryptocurrency. It uses the same underlying technology — distributed ledgers — for a fundamentally different purpose: modernising the regulated financial plumbing that processes trillions of rupees in debt issuances every year. The distinction matters. This is infrastructure, not speculation.

The pilot will need coordination with the Reserve Bank of India, which oversees settlement and payment systems. Pandey indicated that RBI approval is part of the roadmap. The timeline of six to nine months for launch suggests conversations are already advanced.

## What This Means for NRI Investors

For NRIs investing in Indian fixed income — whether through mutual funds, direct bonds or portfolio investment schemes — the tokenisation pilot signals that the market is about to become more liquid, more transparent and potentially far more accessible.

If the pilot succeeds and equity-style disclosure norms are adopted, bond investors will finally have the same information rights that equity investors have enjoyed for decades. The combination of near-instant settlement and lower investment thresholds could unlock a segment of the market that has been effectively invisible to individual investors, including the millions of NRIs who currently limit their Indian exposure to equities and real estate.

India would also become one of the first major economies to bring tokenised bonds into its regulated market infrastructure — ahead of most Western economies that are still in the consultation phase.
